traveler: The Lady of the Lake (Viviane, Niniane, Nimue)
title: Brocéliande to Avalon: the Fairy of the Lake, the Enchanter Bound, and the Sword Given and Taken
years: c. 500-537 (traditional Arthurian chronology; the reign of Arthur, from Merlin's love to the barge at Camlann)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brocéliande, the Fontaine de Barenton
stops.campa: Beneath the pine at the edge of the forest of Brocéliande, the spring called Barenton rises clear from a stone lip, and here, tradition says, Merlin the enchanter first sees Viviane and is undone. She has the mind of a scholar and a face the romances call unmatched; he has the whole craft of Britain in his hands and gives it to her without asking a price. Later poets set the storm-stone here too: strike its face with the golden basin and pour the fountain's water over it, and the sky above Brocéliande breaks into thunder and rain.
suggested_refs: The Fontaine de Barenton itself and the golden basin (bassin d'or) of Chrétien de Troyes' Yvain, ou le Chevalier au Lion, later identified with this spring by local tradition
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Yvain, ou le Chevalier au Lion (12th c.)
Wace, Roman de Rou
Gerald of Wales (Giraldus Cambrensis), Topographia Hibernica (1188)
Encyclopédie de Brocéliande, 'La Fontaine de Barenton'

stops.name: Comper, the palace beneath the lake
stops.campa: For love of Viviane, Merlin raises before the old fortress of Dyonas a palace of crystal set about with gardens where silver-blossomed apple trees never fail. He hides it from every mortal eye behind the plain face of a lake, so perfect an illusion that no one sees the bright halls beneath unless the fairy herself allows it. Viviane rules there as its lady, mistress of waters and of the enchantments Merlin has poured into her, and travelers who pass the shore see only a sheet of quiet water and never guess what shines below it.
suggested_refs: The lake and grounds of the Château de Comper, held by tradition as the site of Viviane's hidden palace
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Lancelot proper (Prose Lancelot)
Destination Brocéliande / Encyclopédie de Brocéliande, 'Château de Comper'
Wikipedia, 'Viviane (Arthurian legend)'

stops.name: Comper, the fostering of Lancelot
stops.campa: A knight lies slain and a queen dies of grief on the shore of Viviane's lake, and the lady lifts their infant son from his dead mother's side before harm can come to him. She carries the child down into the crystal palace and rears him among her waters, teaching him letters, the deeds of the old knights, and the whole art of arms, telling him nothing yet of his father's ruined kingdom. Because her lake has raised him he is named for it ever after: Lancelot du Lac, the boy of the lady whose true name he does not yet know.
suggested_refs: Illuminated Vulgate manuscripts showing Lancelot's underwater education by the Dame du Lac, e.g. BnF Français 122
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the death of King Ban, the fostering of Lancelot)
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book VI

stops.name: Brocéliande, the Tombeau de Merlin
stops.campa: Merlin, who reads every fate but his own, dotes on the lady past all reason and will not be parted from her. She draws his secret arts out of him one by one, makes him swear never to enchant her against her will, and once she holds the whole of his craft in her own hands she wants only to be rid of him. She shows him marvels waiting under a great stone in the forest and persuades him to lie down to see them, then works the charm he taught her, and he who bound half the world cannot unbind this stone, and stays there for all his craft.
stops.quote: he was assotted upon her, that he might not be from her
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter I
suggested_refs: The ruined Neolithic gallery grave in the Forêt de Paimpont known since the 19th century as the Tombeau de Merlin
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter I
Vulgate Merlin Continuation (Suite du Merlin)
Encyclopédie de Brocéliande, 'Le Tombeau de Merlin'

stops.name: Bodmin Moor, Dozmary Pool: the gift of the sword
stops.campa: Merlin brings the new-made king to a still water on the moor and shows him an arm in white samite rising from the middle of the lake, a fair sword bright in its hand. A damosel comes walking on the water itself and tells Arthur the sword is hers to give, if he will grant her a gift when she asks it. He rows out in a little barge, takes the sword and its scabbard, and the arm sinks back beneath the surface without a word. Merlin warns him to prize the scabbard higher than the blade, for while he wears it he cannot bleed to death of any wound.
stops.quote: Sir Arthur, king, said the damosel, that sword is mine, and if ye will give me a gift when I ask it you, ye shall have it.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I, Chapter XXV
suggested_refs: Dozmary Pool on Bodmin Moor, the Cornish moorland lake local tradition names as the giving-place of Excalibur
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I, Chapter XXV
Cornish local tradition, Dozmary Pool

segments.name: The Return of Excalibur: Rival Shores

stops.name: Bodmin Moor, Dozmary Pool: the sword returned
stops.campa: Struck down on the field of Camlann, Arthur commands Sir Bedivere to carry Excalibur to the water's edge and cast it in, though the knight twice hides the blade for its beauty and lies about the deed before the dying king forces him to it a third time. Bedivere hurls the sword out over the pool at last, and an arm and a hand rise from the water, catch it, shake it three times, brandish it, and draw it under the surface for good. Cornish memory has always set this water on the high moor, at Dozmary, where the lake never gives the blade back up.
stops.quote: there came an arm and an hand above the water and met it, and caught it, and so shook it thrice and brandished, and then vanished away the hand with the sword
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter V
suggested_refs: Dozmary Pool, the traditional Cornish site of the sword's return, said (falsely) to have no bottom
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter V
Cornish local tradition, Dozmary Pool

stops.name: The Loe, Cornwall: the rival return
stops.campa: A second Cornish shore claims the same last mile of the story. Where the river Cober is cut from the sea by its bar of storm-thrown shingle, Loe Pool lies long and still below the moor, and the people of this coast have long said it was here, not there, that Bedivere's arm let the blade go and the hand rose to take it. Both waters cannot be right and neither will yield the claim; the sword itself settles nothing, since no one has ever drawn it back up from either lake, and the water keeps its own counsel in both places.
suggested_refs: Loe Bar and Loe Pool near Helston, Cornwall's largest natural lake and Dozmary's rival for the honor
sources: Cornish local tradition, Loe Pool / The Loe
Wikipedia, 'Lady of the Lake'

stops.name: Glastonbury Tor, the vale of Avalon
stops.campa: A black-hooded barge waits at the bank with many fair ladies aboard it, and among them, weeping, is the chief Lady of the Lake herself, called here Nimue, who has long since wed the good knight Sir Pelleas and kept him from danger these many years. They lift the wounded king aboard and row him out toward the west, and Arthur tells Bedivere, watching from the shore, that he goes into the vale of Avalon to be healed of his wound. Whether he lives there still or waits to come again, no one left on the bank can say.
stops.quote: I will into the vale of Avilion to heal me of my grievous wound
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter V
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Tor, held by long tradition (Gerald of Wales, 12th c.) as the Isle of Avalon
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapters V-VI
Gerald of Wales, De Principis Instructione (identification of Glastonbury with Avalon)
